title: Many voices
hook: no single leader speaks for all Sikhs; the Granth and the sangat hold the panth together

segments.voice: Yesterday, women among the five: some gurdwaras include them among the Panj Pyare, some do not. Your line was the conversation continues. Did you leave a door open? Day one thousand three hundred fifty-six.

A reporter calls a gurdwara with a simple request. Can she speak to the head of the Sikh religion? The volunteer who picks up the phone pauses. There's a granthi who reads from the Granth here. There's a committee that runs the building. There's the Akal Takht in Amritsar, whose word carries real weight. But a single person who speaks for every Sikh on earth? The volunteer tries to explain, and the reporter keeps waiting for a name. Today is why there isn't one, and what holds the panth together instead.
screen: `CAN I SPEAK TO THE HEAD?` → `A GRANTHI, A COMMITTEE, A TAKHT.` → `BUT NO ONE VOICE.`

segments.voice: Sikh tradition says that before Guru Gobind Singh died, he ended the line of human Gurus. From then on, the Guru would be the Granth, the scripture, and the Khalsa Panth, the community of Sikhs gathered in the Guru's presence. Sikhs speak of Guru Granth and Guru Panth. That choice shapes everything this week has been about. There are respected bodies. The Akal Takht issues edicts, and they carry weight across the panth. The Shiromani Committee manages historic gurdwaras and published the code of conduct. Taksals and jathas have their own teachers. Local sangats run their own gurdwaras. But none of these is a single head over every Sikh. Authority is spread out, and it's meant to sit under the Granth, not over it. So how does a panth with many voices stay one panth? Gurbani gives a test for a true gathering. On Ang 72, Guru Nanak asks, here in paraphrase, how is the true congregation known? And answers: it is where the one Name is spoken. Not where one leader stands. Where the Name is. That's why a small sangat in a rented hall abroad, a great crowd at the Harmandir, and a family reading together at home can each be the sangat. Many voices is not a design flaw. It's what happens when the Guru is a book everyone can open, and the community is everyone who opens it. The voices sometimes clash. They also keep each other honest.
screen: `GURU GRANTH, GURU PANTH.` · `RESPECTED BODIES, NO SINGLE HEAD.` · `WHERE THE ONE NAME IS SPOKEN.` · `A BOOK EVERYONE CAN OPEN.` · then, large: `MANY VOICES, ONE GURU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen to a voice you don't usually hear. Settle, and breathe. Think of whose voice is usually missing from the circles you're in. Someone younger, or older. Someone quieter. Someone from a different neighborhood, or a different kind of work. Bring one such person to mind. Then plan one small way to hear them this week: a question you'll ask, a talk you'll play, a page you'll read. Breathe with that plan. If you pray, you can hold them before Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
Many voices. No single leader speaks for every Sikh; the Guru Granth Sahib and the sangat, gathered around the Name, hold the panth together. Today's word.
Your line: many voices, one guru. Today, in a group you're part of, notice who hasn't spoken, and make one small space for them. Day one thousand three hundred fifty-six.

howItsDone: Sikhs honor the Guru Granth Sahib as Guru and the Khalsa Panth as the community gathered around it; bodies like the Akal Takht and the Shiromani Committee carry weight, and local sangats run their own gurdwaras, but no single leader speaks for all Sikhs.

options: where the one Name is spoken.
fork.reveal: on Ang 72, the true sangat is known by the Name spoken there. that's part of why many voices can still be one panth.

notes: Ang 72 'satsangat kaisee jaaneeai, jithai eko naam vakhaaneeai' paraphrased as 'how is the true congregation known? it is where the one Name is spoken'. Please confirm the Ang and paraphrase.
Guru Gobind Singh ending the line of human Gurus and vesting Guruship in the Granth and the Khalsa Panth attributed to tradition; no date. Please confirm the 'Guru Granth, Guru Panth' framing.
'Sikhs give them great weight' (of Akal Takht edicts) is a general description, not from a cited text; please confirm.
Shiromani Committee described as managing historic gurdwaras and publishing the code; please confirm wording.

Editor: removed the pope comparison (voice, screen, myth) so no other tradition is used as the foil; 'Sikhs give them great weight' became 'they carry weight across the panth'; 'always meant to sit under' lost 'always'; 'local sangats elect their own committees' became 'run their own gurdwaras', since not every sangat elects.
